standard.title: Mental strategies from known facts
standard.description: extend and apply knowledge of addition and subtraction facts to 20 to develop efficient mental strategies for computation with larger numbers without a calculator
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recall and demonstrate proficiency with addition facts to 20 and related subtraction facts (AC9M2A02). They have not yet applied these facts systematically as a foundation for mental computation with larger numbers.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students extend addition and subtraction facts to 20 into efficient mental strategies for computing with larger numbers.

nodes.label: Extending known facts to larger numbers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use a known fact (e.g. 6+7=13) to derive related calculations (e.g. 16+7=23, 60+70=130) by recognising the place value extension.
nodes.minimum_width: Given three known facts, generate two related larger-number calculations for each and explain the connection.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the extension pattern across a range of addition and subtraction facts to 20; derive mental calculation results for two- and three-digit extensions.
wider: Explore how the extension principle works for subtraction facts as well — connecting 13-7=6 to 130-70=60, 1300-700=600
Investigate how doubles facts (6+6, 7+7) extend to particularly efficient mental strategies for near-doubles in large numbers

response_modes.reason: Students who know 6+7=13 often cannot see why 16+7=23 without re-counting. Seeing the extension pattern across multiple fact families — and across both addition and subtraction — resolves this.

nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising the place value extension from basic facts is the conceptual engine behind all mental strategies in Node 2 — students who do not see why facts extend cannot select appropriate strategies (bridging, partitioning, compensation all rely on this principle) and will revert to counting-based approaches with larger numbers.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The doubles/near-doubles extension and the subtraction parallel provide rich structural insight: students see that place value and basic facts are multiplicatively related, which underpins mental computation throughout upper primary.
success_criteria: Students can state a related larger-number calculation from a given basic fact and explain the connection.
Students can use a known addition fact to derive a larger-number subtraction fact.

nodes.label: Choosing efficient mental strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and apply an efficient mental strategy (bridging, partitioning, compensation) for a given computation with larger numbers.
nodes.minimum_width: Calculate three two-digit additions mentally using a named strategy; explain the strategy chosen for each.
nodes.typical_width: Apply bridging through tens, partitioning and compensation strategies across a range of additions and subtractions; choose the most efficient strategy for each.
wider: Compare two strategies applied to the same problem to determine which is more efficient and why (e.g. bridging vs compensation for 78+24)
Investigate when compensation produces an estimate rather than an exact answer, and when it produces an exact result

response_modes.reason: Mental strategy fluency is built through practice. Once students know the strategies, repeated application in varied contexts is what makes them genuinely 'mental' rather than laboured.
The descriptor calls for a repertoire of strategies. Students need enough practice with each strategy (bridging, partitioning, compensation) to have genuine choice.

success_criteria: Students can calculate a two- or three-digit addition or subtraction mentally using at least one named strategy.
Students can name the strategy they used and explain why they chose it.
